lead: Gradient descent is the engine under every trained network. It measures the slope of the loss with respect to each parameter and moves every parameter a small step in the opposite direction. One fixed step size, the learning rate, serves all of them. Repeat a few thousand times and the loss falls. It exists because the loss of a deep network has millions of dimensions and no closed-form minimum. Training a cheque-clearing image classifier for a bank, or a language model, starts here. This chapter gives the rule, the loop, and the reasons the plain version is not enough.
prereq: You need Unit 1: loss functions, forward propagation and backpropagation, and the idea of a parameter vector.

blocks.text: Stack every weight matrix and bias vector of the model into one vector θ. For a network, θ is simply all the trainable numbers in a single column. Write L(θ) for the average loss over the N training samples.

blocks.where: xᵢ is the i-th input, yᵢ its target, f(xᵢ; θ) the network output, ℓ the per-sample loss (cross-entropy or squared error, Unit 1), and N the number of training samples.

blocks.text: The gradient ∇L(θ) collects the partial derivatives ∂L/∂θⱼ. It points uphill, the direction in which L rises fastest, so we step the other way.

blocks.where: η is the learning rate, a positive scalar. Because ∇L is measured in units of loss per unit of θ, η is measured in units of θ per unit of gradient (that is, θ² per unit of loss). Only when the gradient is dimensionless do η and θ share a unit. Example: with θ in volts and a dimensionless loss, η is in volts². The minus sign is what makes the loss go down.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this batch gradient descent or steepest descent. The word batch refers to using the whole batch of data, all N samples, to compute one gradient.
The loop below is the whole algorithm. Nothing else changes between steps.

items: Forward pass: run all N samples through the network and average the per-sample losses to get L(θ).
Backward pass: backpropagate to get ∂L/∂θⱼ for every parameter. Because L is an average, the gradient is the average of the N per-sample gradients.
Update: apply θ ← θ − η∇L(θ) to every parameter at once.
Test: recompute L. If it has stopped falling, stop. Otherwise go back to the forward pass.

blocks.text: One pass over the training set is an epoch, and here an epoch gives exactly one update. That single fact fixes the cost. With N = 60,000 samples, the size of the MNIST digit set, one step costs 60,000 forward passes plus 60,000 backward passes. A thousand epochs means only a thousand updates.

items: Cost per step. One update needs the full dataset. On a million-image training set that is a million forward and backward passes for one step.
One step size for all parameters. Early layers and late layers, weights and biases, all share η, though their gradient scales differ by orders of magnitude. See 2.4.
Ravines. In a long narrow valley the steep walls force a small η while the floor needs a large one. The path zig-zags across the valley and crawls along it.

Flat regions and saddle points. Where the gradient is near zero the step is near zero, and training stalls even though better ground lies nearby. In high dimensions saddles are far more common than local minima.
Divergence. If η is too large, each step overshoots, the loss jumps, and after a few steps it becomes NaN.
No noise. Every step sees the same data in the same order, so the whole path is fixed by the starting point θ₀.

blocks.text: The loss is not convex, so it can have many local minima. Batch gradient descent has no mechanism inside it to climb out of one.

sections.h3: Bad minima and the usual heuristics

blocks.text: Two old heuristics help against a bad local minimum. The first is random restarts: train from several different starting weights and keep the model with the lowest final loss, which is why the starting spread matters (see 2.6). The second is added noise: jitter the parameters or the gradient estimates so the path can leave a shallow basin.

The noise idea turns out to be the useful one. 2.2 estimates the gradient from one small random batch, so each step is cheap and the estimate is noisy; that noise alone shakes the path out of shallow basins. 2.3 then attacks the ravine problem by smoothing the path with momentum.

figure.caption: Three steps on L(θ) = θ² from θ₀ = 4: with η = 0.1 the steps 4 → 3.2 → 2.56 → 2.048 slide down the bowl; with η = 1.1 the run jumps 4 → −4.8 → 5.76 and the loss climbs 16 → 23.04 → 33.18.

spec.aria: Parabola L equals theta squared with two runs of gradient descent: small steps sliding to the bottom and large steps bouncing outward.

examples.question: Take L(θ) = θ² with a single scalar parameter θ. Start at θ₀ = 4 and run three steps of gradient descent with η = 0.1. List θ₁, θ₂, θ₃ and the factor by which the loss shrinks each step. Then repeat with η = 1.1 and state what happens.
steps: Gradient: ∇L = dL/dθ = 2θ. At θ₀ = 4 the gradient is 8.
Each step is θ ← θ − η(2θ) = (1 − 2η)θ. Here 1 − 2η = 0.8, so θ is multiplied by 0.8 and L = θ² by 0.8² = 0.64 per step.
Now η = 1.1, so 1 − 2η = −1.2. The magnitude grows by 1.2 per step and the sign flips: θ₁ = 4 − 1.1 × 8 = −4.8; the gradient there is −9.6; θ₂ = −4.8 − 1.1 × (−9.6) = −4.8 + 10.56 = 5.76.
The loss went from 16 to 23.04 to 33.18, so it grows without bound: the run diverges.
examples.answer: With η = 0.1 the parameter goes 4 → 3.2 → 2.56 → 2.048 and the loss shrinks by a factor 0.64 per step; with η = 1.1 it goes 4 → −4.8 → 5.76 and the loss diverges.

theta = 4.0
eta = 0.1
for _ in range(3):
    theta = theta - eta * 2.0 * theta
    print(round(theta, 3))
print(round((1 - 2 * eta) ** 2, 2))
theta = 4.0
eta = 1.1
for _ in range(2):
    theta = theta - eta * 2.0 * theta
    print(round(theta, 3))

traps: A loss curve that jumps up and down, or turns into NaN, is divergence from a too-large η. It is not a local minimum.
One epoch is one step in batch gradient descent, not many. Students who assume otherwise get the training time wrong by a factor of N.
Forgetting the 1/N. Summing instead of averaging scales the gradient by N, which is the same as multiplying η by N.
Sign slip: θ ← θ + η∇L climbs the surface. Check by asking whether the loss went down.
η multiplies the gradient, so its size is tied to the gradient's scale. Changing the scale of the inputs changes the gradient and hence the effective step, so η must be re-tuned.

quiz.q: State the batch gradient descent update rule and define every symbol in it.
quiz.a: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ); θ is the full parameter vector, L the average loss over all N samples, ∇L its gradient, and η the learning rate, with the same units as θ.

quiz.q: Why does one epoch give exactly one update in batch gradient descent?
quiz.a: The gradient is the average over all N samples, so no update can be made until every sample has been seen once. The update happens after the pass, not during it.

quiz.q: For L(θ) = θ², start at θ₀ = 2 with η = 0.2. Compute θ₁ and θ₂.
quiz.a: ∇L = 2θ, so at θ₀ the gradient is 4. θ₁ = 2 − 0.2 × 4 = 1.2. Gradient at 1.2 is 2.4, so θ₂ = 1.2 − 0.2 × 2.4 = 0.72.

quiz.q: For L(θ) = θ² with update θ ← (1 − 2η)θ, find the range of η for which the iteration converges to θ = 0.
quiz.a: Convergence needs |1 − 2η| < 1, giving 0 < η < 1. At η = 1 the update is θ ← −θ, so the parameter keeps its magnitude and only flips sign; from θ₀ = 2 it oscillates between 2 and −2, the loss stays at 4, and it never settles. Above 1 it diverges.

quiz.q: Why is a single learning rate a problem in a narrow ravine?
quiz.a: The steep wall needs a small η or the step overshoots. The shallow floor needs a large η to make progress. One η cannot serve both, so the path zig-zags and creeps along the valley.

quiz.q: A student doubles the batch size N without changing anything else and reports that training became unstable. Explain using the update rule.
quiz.a: With code that sums per-sample losses, the gradient is N times the average, so the effective step is Nη. Doubling N doubles that summed gradient again, taking the effective step from Nη to 2Nη, which can be large enough to diverge. Dividing the gradient by the current N restores the averaged update.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the plain form is almost never used to train large models; mini-batch methods with adaptive step sizes and warmup-plus-decay schedules took over. Second-order ideas such as Newton's method and L-BFGS use curvature but cost too much at millions of parameters. Research now looks at the shape of the loss landscape, in particular whether flat minima generalize better than sharp ones. Search for loss landscape visualization, sharp versus flat minima, and learning rate warmup and cosine decay.
